\(v_z\)
 and a constant vertical speed 
\(v_{x0} = (\mu_s dB/dx)\,(l_2/mv_z)\)

\(v_x\)

\[\delta_2 = l_3 v_{x0}/v_z\]
 This yields

 . Thus we obtain

. This gives for 
\(\vec{B}(x,y)\)
 
\[\begin{equation}
\frac{\mu I_0}{2\pi}\left[\frac{\hat{k}\times(x\hat{\imath} + (y-a)\hat{\jmath}}{r_1^2} - \frac{\hat{k}\times(x\hat{\imath} + (y+a)\hat{\jmath}}{r_2^2}\right] \tag{1}
\end{equation}\]

\[\begin{equation}
= \frac{\mu I_0\, a}{\pi r_1^2 r_2^2}\left[2xy\hat{\jmath} + (x^2 - y^2 + a^2)\hat{\imath}\right] \tag{2}

 The 
\(\hat{\imath}\)
 component is zero. Thus

First Alternative Solution


We can show in general that the field at 
any

\((x_c, y)\)

\(\sqrt{x_c^2 + a^2}\)
. The equation of a circle with 
\((x_c, 0)\)

\(\sqrt{x_c^2 + a^2}\)

\[(x - x_c)^2 + y^2 = x_c^2 + a^2\]
 or 
\[\begin{equation}
x^2 - 2\,x\,x_c + y^2 = a^2 \tag{3}
\end{equation}\]
 If at the point 
\((x_c, y_c)\)

\(\hat{\jmath}\)

\(\hat{\imath}\)

\((x_c, 0)\)

\(y_c\)

\[x_c^2 - y_c^2 + a^2 = 0\]

\[\begin{equation}
y_c^2 = x_c^2 + a^2 \tag{4}
\end{equation}\]
 Now consider a line joining C 
\((x_c, 0)\)
 to any point 
\(P_C(x,y)\)
 lying on the circle given by eq.(3). The radial vector is 
\(\vec{CP}_C = (x - x_c)\hat{\imath} + y\hat{\jmath}\)
. The magnetic field at 
\(P_C\)
 is 
\[\propto \vec{B}(x,y,0) = \left(\frac{\mu I_0}{\pi}\right)\left(2xy\hat{\jmath} + (x^2 - y^2 + a^2)\hat{\imath}\right)\]
 To show that they are in the same direction, we evaluate the cross product, 
\(\vec{CP}_C \times \vec{B}\)
. The cross product is proportional to 
\(\hat{n}\)
 which is a unit vector along the direction which is normal to both 
\(CP_C\)
 and 
\(\vec{B}\)
 and is along 
\(\hat{k}\)
 
\[\vec{CP}_C \times \vec{B} \propto (2\,x\,y(x - x_c) - y(x^2 - y^2 + a^2))\,\hat{k}\]
 which simplifies to 
\[y(x^2 - 2x\,x_c + y^2 - a^2)\hat{k}\]
 Using eq.(3), this is zero, proving the result.

To show that the field lines are radial over the circe one may merely show the proportionality of the components of the field and the radius vector. The radius vector is 
\((x - x_c)\hat{\imath} + y\hat{\jmath}\)
 while the magnetic field is proportional to 
\((x^2 - y^2 + a^2)\hat{\imath} + 2xy\hat{\jmath}\)
. Thus 
\[\begin{align*}
\frac{y}{2xy} &= \frac{1}{2x}\\
&\text{and}\\
\frac{x - x_c}{x^2 - y^2 + a^2} &= \frac{1}{2x}
\end{align*}\]
 The last step is obtained by observing that the equation of the circle is 
\((x - x_c)^2 + y^2 = x_c^2 + a^2\)
.
